opus-5.5.text:
I think skills are one of the most practical answers we have right now to a very real problem: a general model knows a lot about the world, but it knows almost nothing about *your* company.

When a new employee joins, they're already smart and competent. What they lack is the organizational context: how this team writes a design doc, who has to sign off before something ships, which internal tools are trusted and which are legacy, what "done" actually means here. Nobody teaches that by retraining the person's brain. You hand them a handbook, some templates, a few examples, and you let them pick it up while working.

Skills play that same role for agents. A skill packages a procedure, the relevant instructions, maybe some scripts or reference files, and the agent loads it when the task calls for it. So the norms live outside the model weights, in something the enterprise can read, edit, version, and audit. That matters a lot. If your compliance process changes next quarter, you don't want to fine-tune a model; you want to change a document.

There's also an efficiency point. You can't stuff an organization's entire tacit knowledge into every prompt; the context would explode and the model would get confused. Skills are loaded on demand, so the agent carries a lightweight index of what it *can* do and only pulls in the details when it needs them. That's much closer to how people work: you don't memorize the expense policy, you know where to look.

But I'd add a caveat. Skills capture what can be written down. A lot of organizational norms are tacit: judgment calls, unwritten priorities, knowing when a rule should bend. Writing good skills forces companies to make some of that explicit, which is valuable in itself, but there will always be a gap. Closing that gap probably requires the agent to learn from feedback over time, so it isn't just following the handbook but gradually developing something like experience inside the organization.

So my view is: skills are the onboarding layer. They're necessary, they're the right abstraction for now, and they make agents governable. But the long-term goal is agents that can turn their own experience in an organization into new skills, rather than relying only on humans to write everything down for them.

r001.rationale: Skills are described as packages of procedures and instructions that the agent loads when a task calls for them.

r002.rationale: The response says a general model knows little about a particular company, but does not explain that these norms are absent from pre-training because they accumulate internally.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning from feedback over time, but does not identify repeated task interactions as the means of teaching organizational norms.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest way to answer is to start with what a skill actually is, because the word gets used loosely. A skill, in the way we've been building them, is a packaged piece of procedural knowledge: here is how we do this task, here are the steps, here are the tools you call, here are the conditions under which you stop and ask someone. It's closer to a runbook than it is to a prompt.

And when you look at it that way, you realize that most of what an enterprise calls "culture" or "norms" is actually tacit procedure. Nobody writes down that in this company you never send a number to a client without someone in finance looking at it first. Nobody writes down that when legal says "we'll review it" that means a two-week delay, so you plan around it. New employees learn this by making mistakes and getting corrected. An agent has no onboarding period. It arrives on day one with a very strong general prior about how the world works, and that prior is usually wrong for your specific company in a hundred small ways.

So the role of skills, for me, is that they're the mechanism by which the organization's implicit knowledge becomes explicit and transferable. The thing I find interesting is that the act of writing a skill forces the humans to articulate what they actually do. Very often the first version of a skill is wrong, not because the agent misread it, but because the person who wrote it described an idealized process rather than the real one. The agent follows the written version faithfully, something breaks, and that's when the team discovers the gap between their documentation and their behavior. The agent becomes a kind of mirror.

The second thing I'd say is that skills give you a layer of governance that a fine-tuned model can't. If you bake norms into weights, you can't inspect them, you can't version them, and when the policy changes you have to retrain. If norms live in skills, then the compliance team can read them, the engineering lead can diff them, and when the approval threshold changes from ten thousand to fifty thousand, you edit a file. For an enterprise that matters enormously. The model is a general capability; the skills are where the company lives.

Where I'd push back on the hype a little is that skills don't replace judgment. They encode the known paths. The hard cases are the ones no one anticipated, and there the question is whether the skill tells the agent to escalate rather than improvise. The best skills I've seen are almost conservative: a lot of the content is about boundaries, when to stop, who to hand off to. That's actually how you'd describe a good junior employee too. You don't want them to be creative with the expense policy. You want them to know it, follow it, and ask when it's unclear.

r001.rationale: Skills are described as packaged procedural knowledge with steps, tools, and stopping conditions for the agent to follow.

r002.rationale: The response says an agent's general prior may not fit company-specific norms, but does not explain that those norms are missing from pre-training data because they accumulate internally.

r003.rationale: The response discusses writing skills and following their procedures, but does not identify repeated task interactions as a way to teach organizational norms.

astra-6.text:
I think skills can serve as a bridge between an agent’s general capabilities and the way a particular organization works. Knowing how to write a report doesn’t mean knowing what your company considers a good report, who needs to review it, or what information can be shared.

A useful skill makes those expectations explicit. It can describe the workflow, provide examples, and explain when the agent should act independently and when it should ask someone. In that sense, you’re teaching not just how to complete a task, but how to participate in the organization.

But organizational norms aren’t always consistent or written down. So creating skills also forces people to clarify their own assumptions. Is this a firm rule, a team preference, or simply how one person has always done things? Those distinctions matter. Otherwise, you risk turning an informal habit into a rigid instruction.

I’d treat skills as living guidance: specific enough to shape behavior, with clear ownership and a way to improve them when real situations reveal gaps.

r001.rationale: The response says skills make expectations explicit and shape behavior, but it does not clearly characterize them as specifications for the model to execute.

r002.rationale: It discusses norms as inconsistent or unwritten, but does not say they are absent from pre-training data because they are accumulated internally within enterprises.

r003.rationale: It mentions real situations revealing gaps, but does not identify repeated task interactions as a way to teach norms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think skills are a way to turn an enterprise’s organizational norms into instructions an agent can actually follow. Those norms often live in people’s heads: how to review a document, when to ask for approval, what information can be shared, and who should be involved in a decision.

A skill can capture that context alongside a workflow, examples, and the tools needed to carry it out. So the agent learns more than how to complete a task; it learns how this organization expects that task to be done.

But writing a skill doesn’t automatically make the norm clear or correct. You still need people to resolve conflicting expectations, define where the skill applies, and update it as practices change. I see skills as a practical bridge between organizational knowledge and agent behavior, with human judgment still responsible for maintaining that bridge.

r001.rationale: It describes skills as instructions that capture norms and workflows for an agent to follow.

r002.rationale: It says norms often live in people’s heads, but does not explain that they are absent from pre-training because they accumulate internally within enterprises.

r003.rationale: It does not identify repeated task interactions as a way to teach norms.
